blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: What population structure is, how to read an age/sex pyramid, and what a high dependent population means for a country.

blocks.heading: What structure means
blocks.text: Population structure is the make-up of a population by age groups and sex, shown on an age/sex pyramid. The bars are age groups, youngest at the bottom, with males on one side and females on the other. The shape is a record of the birth and death rates a country has had: a high birth rate builds a wide base of children, and an old, low-mortality population builds a top-heavy pyramid. A wide base comes from a high birth rate and marks a growing population; a narrow base with a top-heavy shape comes from a low birth rate and an ageing one, and as a falling birth rate works through, the base narrows first and the ageing follows decades later. Describing structure means naming the broad groups and their proportions, young dependants aged 0-14, the economically active aged 15-64, and elderly dependants aged 65 and over, not just the outline of the drawing.

blocks.heading: Reading a pyramid
blocks.text: Two reading errors are common. The first is describing the shape, wide base, narrow top, and stopping there, when the structure is the groups and their shares. The second is reading one bar or one side: an age group's share is males plus females in that group, so a single bar undercounts it. A pyramid answer names the groups, gives their proportions and adds both sexes.

blocks.heading: Dependancy and its weight
blocks.text: The dependent population is the people too young or too old to work, who rely on the economically active, and the dependency ratio compares them with the people of working age. A high ratio means each worker supports more people, and the burden lands differently by kind: a mostly young dependent population needs schools, clinics and feeding, and a mostly old one needs pensions, health care and carers. In both cases the active group must fund its own households and the dependants' too, which is why a high dependent population shifts a country's spending whether the dependants are at the bottom of the pyramid or the top.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The birth and death rates that build a pyramid are the ones defined in topic 1.1, and Niger, this topic's case study, is the high-growth case study there too. Population density and distribution, topic 1.4, show where the people in the pyramid actually live.
